⚡️Cognition just became heavy industry, and this article is the disclosure event. 

The dominant truth: water is the binding constraint of the AI buildout because it is the one input that cannot be arbitraged across geography, and everything else in the stack can. 

Capital moves at wire speed, chips ship, power gets built in eighteen months, but water is watershed-local, legally encumbered, and politically primal. The line in the piece that carries the whole thesis is the Nevada-Michigan sentence: a dry river in one basin cannot be offset by abundance in another. Every other constraint on AI is fungible. This one has coordinates.

RECs are claims that decouple the legal representation from the physical draw, fiat logic applied to electrons: buy a certificate in one geography, consume wet megawatts in another, report “water positive.” The 3x indirect multiple at Google and 20x at Meta means every published datacenter water number understates the true draw by an order of magnitude, which sets up a revision bomb: the coming political fight will be fought with numbers that suddenly get twenty times worse on restatement, and narrative risk of that shape never reprices gradually.

The mechanism nobody in the thread will name: the buildout’s speed is its water bill. The gas-heavy backbone got chosen because gas deploys fast, and thermoelectric generation is evaporative by design, wet cooling towers boiling rivers into the sky to make tokens. Behind-the-meter turbines, the current fashion for dodging interconnect queues, are the maximum-water path. Solar and wind consume almost nothing, but they lost the race on velocity. The industry selected the water-intensive route as the price of speed, which means the constraint tightens on the same schedule as the capex, not after it.

Water rights are the oldest continuously litigated property claims in America, prior appropriation doctrine, agricultural seniority, century-old compacts, and the claimants vote. Datacenter siting fights are already the hottest local politics in a dozen states. Now overlay the newest fact on the board: the federal government is taking equity in the AI complex. The sovereign shareholder acquires a direct financial interest in overriding local water objections, and the collision is fully predictable, federal preemption of water and land constraints for “strategic AI infrastructure” against the one resource where local claims are oldest and voters care most. The referee owns the team, and the next thing the team needs is the other team’s river.

Burry himself is detection-layer signal with unauthorized timing, per his entire career: the structural flaw he names is real and the pop he implies is not scheduled by it. And the constraint he is holding actually cuts against his trade in one decisive respect. Physical rationing does not deflate the sector, it concentrates it. Whoever locked water rights, interconnects, and cooling capacity early converts a commodity input into a moat, and scarcity becomes the incumbents’ pricing power. The bear case for aggregate capex fantasies and the bull case for resource-secured hyperscalers are the same fact. Rationing picks winners; it does not pick zero.

The asset implication closes the loop: water is the most underpriced scarce atom on earth, agriculture pays near zero for senior rights while the marginal industrial user now bidding is the most valuable industry in history. 

That spread closes. 

Water rights, basins with surplus, cooling-adjacent infrastructure, and the political jurisdictions that own wet geography move from externality to asset class inside this cycle.

Before the Big-Bang, Life After Death, and an Old Movie

In the movie “Contact” with Judie Foster, the spiritual figure in there (played by Matthew McConauhey) pointed out that the one question people ask most, namely the one about meaning, science has not answered so far.
Connected with this question are undoubtedly also the questions about
“What was before the creation of the universe?”
and
“Is there a life after death?”

Knowing that one day my children would ask me those questions, I decided - about 20 years ago - to try and find answers.
This little project of mine ended in a book [342, 319], which I published under a different name and two papers, which I kept secret for over 10 years and finally published in very rigorous mathematical form (after all, I wanted to do the job right) [360, 362].
I found that answers to all three questions are possible, but complex (no surprise there).
The questions about “the time before time” [360] and “the life after death” [362] belong together and lead to a huge field of possibilities laying beyond classical science (which is based on extremal and variation principles).
The meaning or purpose question on the other hand is a little bit trickier and I hope you can forgive me when I refer to the book (rest assured, it does not contain math – well, one of them [342] does not).
And what does this all have to do with real life and applications?
Well, just think about the so-called “virtual particles” and fields or undetectable potentials, still creating effects. Think about quantum computing and those strange states in limbo, we are unable to access, but we know they do exist (in some strange way, classical science cannot describe).
Think about the “ghosts” in AI.
Think about the way you come up with great ideas, not knowing where those suddenly came from.
Think…

…and have a wonderful day.
Norbert

Reward-guided diffusion: reinforcement learning steers generative models toward novel, stable crystals

Anyone who trains generative models knows the tension. A diffusion model fit by maximum likelihood learns to reproduce its training distribution, so it samples what looks familiar. In materials discovery, though, the interesting compounds sit in the low-probability tails, the underexplored regions where genuinely new structures live. Sampling more of the same is exactly what you do not want.

Hyunsoo Park and Aron Walsh reframe this as a post-training problem. Instead of nudging outputs with heuristics like classifier-free guidance, they fine-tune the model with reinforcement learning, optimizing explicit rewards rather than data likelihood. The move that makes it tractable: they run diffusion in a compressed VAE latent space, which turns the awkward mix of discrete atom types and continuous coordinates into a homogeneous action space where policy gradients behave.

The engine is GRPO, the same group-relative policy optimization behind recent reasoning LLMs, here driving a denoising diffusion policy. The reward is multi-objective and, crucially, verifiable: a creativity term for uniqueness and novelty, a stability term using a machine-learning force field as a fast proxy for DFT energy above the convex hull, and a diversity term that blocks mode collapse.

The payoff is a clean shift of the Pareto frontier. On the Alex-MP-20 benchmark, their metastable-unique-novel score jumps from 15.9% to 61.3%, novelty climbs from 62.3% to 97.5%, and metastability still rises from 51.2% to 72.1%. Novelty and stability usually trade off, and here RL buys both at once. The same framework handles inverse design too: targeting a 3 eV bandgap, RL keeps chemical validity intact while classifier-free guidance collapses to near-zero.

For discovery pipelines in batteries, catalysis, or semiconductors, the practical takeaway is that a verifiable reward plus policy optimization can redirect a generative model toward candidates worth synthesizing, not merely plausible ones. Swap the reward and the same machinery targets ionic conductivity, formation energy, or a specific gap, giving a modular path from "generates something reasonable" to "generates what the program actually needs."

Paper: Park et al., Nature Machine Intelligence (2026), CC BY 4.0 | https://t.co/4cwgBOxl0F

Boost real-robot policy success & speed
using only cheap simulation, 
without needing any extra real data: 

- 2.4× success + 37% faster execution
- Half-day iteration with new retry behaviors

Real-robot imitation policies for dexterous manipulationby learning to steer diffusion or flow models in simulation without collecting extra real-world data.

The approach freezes the base policy trained on real data and uses RL only to select successful latent inputs within the policy’s support, avoiding sim-reality gaps from contact dynamics that plague full finetuning.

Results show 2.4x higher real-world success rates and 37% faster execution across tasks like block picking, with quick half-day iteration from setup to deployment while enabling retry behaviors absent in base policies.

A paper worth knowing about if you're into quant trading and generative AI:

TRADES: Generating Realistic Market Simulations with Diffusion Models

Authors: Berti, Prenkaj, Velardi (Sapienza University of Rome + TU Munich)

What's inside:
> A transformer-based diffusion model for generating orders in the Limit Order Book (LOB) - realistic simulation of the market order book
> Two key metrics - realism (how close it is to real market behavior) and responsiveness (how the market reacts to an agent's actions)
> Results: ×3.27 and ×3.48 improvement over SoTA on the predictive score across two stocks
> DeepMarket - the first open-source Python framework for deep-learning-based LOB simulations
> Comes with a synthetic LOB dataset generated by the model itself

A step toward backtesting trading strategies and training RL agents on data that behaves like a real market instead of random noise.
